title: Rapid reversal of septic shock and its harmful host response

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliably deployable treatment, or rapidly selected combination of treatments, that reverses septic shock: restoring effective circulation and preventing progressive organ dysfunction while preserving the immune defenses needed to fight infection. Its intended scope includes early emergency care. A single dose that works for every patient within minutes remains an aspiration, not a demonstrated capability.

One relevant approach targets the vascular component of shock. The supplied AdrenOSS-2 report describes an investigational strategy using adrecizumab, a non-neutralizing antibody directed at adrenomedullin, with the aim of supporting the endothelial barrier—the cell layer lining blood vessels—and limiting vascular dysfunction. This is one possible component of the broader innovation; studying this pathway does not establish comprehensive reversal of the harmful host response or preservation of immune defenses.

significance.text: If a treatment could rapidly restore circulation and prevent progressive organ failure across a substantial range of septic-shock patients, it would add a major emergency-care capability. The vascular-treatment rationale connects maintenance or repair of the endothelial barrier with the possibility of reducing organ dysfunction. Reduced need for prolonged organ support would be a plausible consequence of successfully preventing organ failure, but it was not established as an adrecizumab benefit in the supplied trial.

Conditional synthesis: successful early reversal could make stabilization more dependable and reduce the burden of prolonged critical illness. The magnitude of those benefits would depend on how quickly treatment works, which patients benefit, whether recovery persists, and whether treatment introduces immune or infectious complications. A result confined to a narrowly selected subgroup could still be valuable, while supporting a narrower claim than broadly effective septic-shock rescue.

Conceptual limit: stabilizing the body's response to infection does not itself establish elimination of the infection. Effective antimicrobial treatment and control of an infection source might still be required. Likewise, rapid improvement in blood pressure alone would not demonstrate durable organ recovery, survival benefit, or preservation of immune function. These are distinct parts of the proposed clinical achievement.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability in this concept is dependable, rapid reversal of dangerous shock with sustained organ protection and acceptable effects on host defenses. The supplied report supports the difficulty posed by heterogeneous septic-shock populations and the rationale for personalized treatment. It does not establish that one intervention can deliver the whole capability, or determine whether that broader goal remained unmet across the field on November 1, 2026.

Patient selection is a concrete scientific and operational barrier. A targeted treatment must identify patients whose disease biology is responsive, and selection must happen early enough to alter the course of shock. In AdrenOSS-2, the biomarker assay usually took less than two hours, infusion took approximately one hour, and treatment began a median of 8.5 hours after vasopressor initiation. These timings demonstrate a studied selection-and-treatment workflow, but do not establish deployment within minutes.

Proposed engineering and biological requirements: a deployable system would need reliable selection under emergency-care conditions, timely delivery alongside other treatment, and a response that persists beyond initial circulatory improvement. It would also need to avoid suppressing necessary immune defenses. The original research's account of different pathogens and changing immune and vascular responses is useful as a motivation for this broad goal, but the supplied evidence does not adequately establish that complete biological account or show that immune preservation has been achieved.

A further barrier is converting a plausible vascular mechanism into convincing clinical benefit. The supplied phase IIa trial was not powered to prove efficacy, did not show a significant benefit on its Sepsis Support Index, and left substantial uncertainty around mortality. Larger confirmatory evidence would be needed to distinguish a reproducible therapeutic effect from preliminary or exploratory signals.

current_state.text: The 2021 AdrenOSS-2 report, published on October 4, described a randomized, multicenter, phase IIa biomarker-guided trial of adrecizumab in 301 patients with septic shock. The study was conducted in intensive care units. It demonstrates that a targeted vascular-response strategy can be selected using a biomarker and tested clinically; it does not demonstrate rapid emergency-department deployment or the complete proposed rescue capability.

The trial found no overt safety signal, but this does not establish definitive safety or preservation of immune defenses. Reported 28-day mortality was 23.9% with adrecizumab versus 27.7% with placebo, with a hazard ratio of 0.84, a 95% confidence interval of 0.53–1.31, and p=0.44. The interval permits both meaningful benefit and harm, so the comparison did not establish a reliable survival benefit. The authors explicitly stated that the trial was not powered to prove clinical efficacy.

The Sepsis Support Index showed no significant benefit. Exploratory findings involving the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score require confirmation because of missing data and multiple testing without adjustment. These findings do not establish durable organ protection. Conversely, an inconclusive preliminary trial does not prove that the vascular strategy cannot work.

The article also describes earlier preclinical findings in which modulation of the adrenomedullin pathway improved endothelial homeostasis, organ function, and survival in models of septic shock. Those findings provide a mechanistic rationale, not proof of human efficacy. The underlying animal papers were not separately supplied for review.

Evidence scope: the supplied review assessed the full main article and obtained the numerical findings from its prose; linked supplementary files and figure images were not inspected. The source index records a complete, untruncated main-article extraction without reported extraction issues. The supplied search record is empty, so this dated evidence cannot establish the full field's status on November 1, 2026, or whether later studies changed the assessment.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: randomized multicenter trials beginning early in emergency care should show a clinically substantial improvement in survival and durable organ function when the intervention is added to current treatment. Investigators should prospectively define what counts as substantial, the duration of follow-up, and the acceptable time from presentation through selection to treatment. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Multicenter trials demonstrate substantial survival and durable organ function gains

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and reproducibility requirements: trials should prespecify infection sources and patient groups, report which groups benefit or fail to benefit, and confirm the result in independent populations and care settings. If biomarker selection is necessary, both its predictive usefulness and its real-world turnaround time should be demonstrated. Finite trials would establish effectiveness across the populations and conditions tested; they could not prove literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Subgroup benefits are reported and independently reproduced across care settings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and durability requirements: evaluation should measure immune complications, recurrent infection, treatment interactions, sustained organ recovery, and continued need for organ support. Early circulatory improvement should be linked to outcomes that matter to patients. Claims that necessary immune defenses are preserved would require specific evidence beyond the absence of an overt safety signal.
completion_criteria.label: Immune safety and sustained organ recovery are explicitly evaluated

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: a convincing demonstration should state the treatment window, selection rules, delivery time, care resources required, and dependence on antimicrobial treatment or source control. If benefit is limited to a subgroup or requires several hours of selection and treatment, that remains a meaningful achievement but would support a correspondingly bounded capability rather than a single-dose rescue for everyone within minutes.
completion_criteria.label: Treatment windows and deployment requirements are explicitly stated

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: EMR-05, “A portable, broad-spectrum emergency diagnostic system,” has the closest operational overlap because rapid diagnosis or patient selection could help direct septic-shock treatment. Diagnostic capability and therapeutic reversal remain separate achievements: identifying a patient or treatment target does not establish that shock can be reversed.

Roster-based synthesis: EMR-03, “Field treatment that safely stops inaccessible internal bleeding,” and EMR-04, “Inexpensive, universally compatible emergency blood replacement,” also concern restoration or preservation of effective circulation. Their principal targets are bleeding and blood replacement; EMR-06 concerns infection-associated shock and the harmful host response. Shared stabilization goals do not make the treatments interchangeable.

Roster-based synthesis: EMR-01, “Reversible emergency metabolic suspension,” EMR-02, “Neurologically intact recovery after prolonged untreated cardiac arrest,” EMR-08, “Non-surgical rescue oxygenation for otherwise unmanageable airways,” and EMR-11, “Acute rescue and repair of injured vital tissue,” overlap through preservation of vital organs during emergencies. Their respective aims—temporarily reducing metabolic demand, recovery after arrest, rescue oxygenation, and tissue rescue or repair—remain distinct from reversing septic shock. Organ protection would be an outcome of successful EMR-06 treatment, without establishing those other capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: EMR-07, “Broad-spectrum emergency antidote platform,” shares the ambition of rapidly selecting effective treatment across diverse causes. Its antidote framing should not be transferred literally to sepsis: the proposed septic-shock capability must address a harmful host response while retaining needed defenses, and vascular stabilization alone does not establish removal of the infectious cause.

Roster-based synthesis: EMR-09, “Effective early prevention of post-traumatic stress disorder after emergency care,” and EMR-10, “Rapid, potent non-opioid treatment for severe acute pain,” share the emergency-care setting but address different outcomes. Neither psychological prevention nor analgesia demonstrates circulatory rescue, and successful septic-shock treatment would not establish either capability.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the field-wide status of rapid septic-shock reversal on November 1, 2026; later clinical developments were not assessed.
Whether this vascular-targeted strategy produces a reproducible survival or durable organ-function benefit remains unresolved by the supplied trial.
Preservation of necessary immune defenses, recurrent-infection risks, and a complete account of changing immune responses are not established by the supplied evidence.
The effective patient groups, treatment window, and feasibility of selection and delivery within minutes remain undemonstrated.
A future protocol must define clinically substantial benefit, follow-up duration, acceptable selection time, and the breadth of populations to be tested.
Linked supplements, figure images, and underlying preclinical papers were not inspected in the supplied review.

brief.title: Restoring blood flow when infection overwhelms the body
possible: People with septic shock—a dangerous failure of circulation caused by the body's response to infection—could receive treatment that quickly restores blood flow and prevents worsening organ damage. Doctors could choose a treatment or combination early in emergency care while preserving the body's ability to fight infection.
why: For patients and families, dependable early recovery could mean better survival and less prolonged critical illness. Emergency teams could stabilize patients more reliably, with fewer people needing extended support to keep their organs working.

sources.who: Pierre-François Laterre, Peter Pickkers and colleagues
sources.showed: A preliminary trial tested adrecizumab, a drug intended to support the lining of blood vessels, in 301 patients. It found no clear safety warning but did not establish a survival benefit.
sources.quote: Adrecizumab was well tolerated (one interruption, no hemodynamic alteration)
sources.cited_for: The trial supports testing a treatment aimed at blood vessel function in selected patients.
sources.not_established: It did not establish rapid rescue, lasting organ protection or preservation of infection-fighting defenses.

sources.who: D. Annane and colleagues for the CRICS-TRIGGERSEP Network
sources.showed: In a randomized trial, hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone, two steroid medicines, reduced deaths and increased days without organ failure. Raised blood sugar was more common.
sources.quote:
The rate of serious adverse events did not differ significantly between the two groups, but
hyperglycemia was more common in hydrocortisone-plus-fludrocortisone group.
sources.cited_for: The trial demonstrates that treatment can improve survival and some organ outcomes in selected patients with septic shock.
sources.not_established: It did not establish rescue within minutes, lasting organ recovery or preservation of necessary immune defenses.

sources.showed: Personalized circulation treatment used capillary refill time—the time skin takes to regain color after pressure—to guide care. It improved a combined outcome, mainly through shorter organ support.
sources.quote:
Among patients with early septic shock, a personalized
hemodynamic resuscitation protocol targeting capillary refill time was superior to usual care
for the primary composite outcome, primarily due to a lower duration of vital support.
sources.cited_for: The trial supports tailoring early circulation treatment to the patient's condition.
sources.not_established: The combined outcome does not by itself establish a survival benefit or comprehensive reversal of the harmful response to infection.

shown: D. Annane and colleagues showed that a steroid combination improved survival and days without organ failure. The ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 investigators showed that personalized circulation treatment shortened the need for organ support. These are partial advances toward rapid, dependable rescue.
missing: A dependable early treatment that rapidly restores circulation and keeps organs recovering has yet to be demonstrated.
Fast patient selection must reliably identify who will benefit under emergency-care conditions.
Specific evidence must show that treatment preserves infection-fighting defenses and avoids recurrent infection.

milestones.label: Trials show substantial survival and lasting organ recovery
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials across hospitals would have to show substantial survival and lasting organ-function gains when treatment starts early in emergency care. This would establish benefits beyond a temporary rise in blood pressure.

milestones.label: Patient-group benefits repeat across care settings
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to identify which patient groups benefit and independently reproduce those results across settings, including any selection test's accuracy and speed. This would establish who can reliably benefit.

milestones.label: Immune safety and sustained organ recovery are evaluated
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to measure immune complications, recurrent infection, treatment interactions, lasting organ recovery and continued support needs. This would test whether early improvement persists without weakening infection defenses.

milestones.label: Treatment timing and practical requirements are defined
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to state treatment windows, selection rules, delivery times, required resources and dependence on infection treatment. This would define where and how the rescue can work.

uncertain: Whether targeting blood vessel function with adrecizumab produces a reproducible survival or lasting organ benefit remains unresolved.
How large and long-lasting a benefit must be to count as successful rescue remains to be defined.

page.title: Host-directed reversal of septic shock
page.definition: A treatment of the patient's response to infection that reverses septic shock, the circulatory failure accompanying sepsis. In adults receiving infection treatment, it restores peripheral perfusion during 6 hours, ends dependence on blood-pressure-raising drugs for at least 24 hours, and improves organ recovery and survival without increasing secondary infections.

goal.need: APROCCHSS enrolled 1,241 adults with septic shock. Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone improved survival, but 43.0% of treated patients died within 90 days. The treatment also increased mean days alive without organ failure during the first 28 days from 12 to 14. These outcomes provide separate benchmarks for survival and organ recovery.

figures.caption: APROCCHSS: deaths within 90 days
figures.note: Both groups received usual treatment for septic shock.

completion.title: Independent trials establish rapid shock reversal, organ recovery and survival without increased infection.
completion.criterion: Independent multicentre randomized trials of the same host-directed strategy in adults show more patients attaining capillary refill time ≤3 seconds during 6 hours, earlier mean arterial pressure ≥60 mm Hg sustained for ≥24 hours without vasopressors, more days alive with SOFA <6 through day 28, and lower 90-day mortality than usual care. SOFA scores dysfunction in six organ systems. The trials also exclude increased secondary-infection risk: the upper 95% confidence limit for its risk ratio is ≤1, counting new infections arising ≥48 hours after randomization. This joint test, including the infection-safety bound, is Atlas-defined.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; synthesis of ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 and APROCCHSS endpoints, with an explicitly Atlas-defined infection-safety bound and independent confirmation requirement.
completion.basis: Searches of FDA materials, Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidance and research priorities, BARDA product profiles and published sepsis protocols found no joint rapid-reversal, organ-recovery, survival and immune-safety standard. The component clinical endpoints come from published protocols. The joint requirement and infection-safety bound are Atlas choices. Peripheral perfusion and infection outcomes do not establish preservation of every immune function.

milestones.title: A host-response treatment improves cardiac output within 3 hours in an infection-induced animal model.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a treatment effect on cardiac output during the 3-hour observation period in the published rat protocol, using its P<0.05 significance criterion. In 2019, adrecizumab, 2 mg/kg intravenously 24 hours after caecal ligation and puncture, increased cardiac output versus untreated septic rats (P=0.006). There were 71 rats undergoing sepsis induction overall and at least 7 animals in each principal treatment group; 28% died before treatment. This experiment did not establish survival benefit after treatment.
milestones.set_by: Blet and colleagues, published experimental protocol and statistical criterion; specific to their rat model, not a general preclinical qualification standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

milestones.title: A host-response drug reaches first administration in humans in a phase I investigation.
milestones.criterion: Administer an investigational host-response drug to humans in a phase I study assessing pharmacology and adverse effects. Geven and colleagues reported two randomized studies in 2018, each enrolling 24 healthy men: first administration in humans and experimental endotoxaemia. Each study tested adrecizumab at 0.5, 2 and 8 mg/kg, with 6 active-drug recipients and 2 placebo recipients per dose cohort, and 90-day follow-up. Neither study tested treatment of clinical septic shock.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a), definition of phase I; applied here as a development-stage definition, not evidence of FDA authorization of the Dutch studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: A biomarker-selected host-response treatment reaches randomized phase II testing in septic-shock patients.
milestones.criterion: Complete randomized treatment of patients selected using the AdrenOSS-2 eligibility thresholds: bioactive adrenomedullin >70 pg/mL and <12 hours since vasopressor initiation. The 2021 report included 301 patients. Severe treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 105/149 adrecizumab recipients and 108/152 placebo recipients; mortality benefit was not established. Separately, ImmunoSep analysed 276 biomarker-selected sepsis patients, not exclusively septic-shock patients: its ≥1.4-point mean SOFA improvement endpoint by day 9 occurred in 46/131 versus 26/145 patients (P=.002), without established mortality benefit.
milestones.set_by: AdrenOSS-2 investigators, NCT03085758, published eligibility and phase II protocol; ImmunoSep supplies additional patient-level evidence for biomarker-directed treatment.
milestones.threshold_quote: Patients with adrenomedullin above 70 pg/mL, < 12 h of vasopressor start for septic shock were eligible.

milestones.title: Personalized resuscitation increases attainment of capillary refill time ≤3 seconds during 6 hours.
milestones.criterion: Reach the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 peripheral-perfusion target during its 6-hour intervention: capillary refill time ≤3 seconds after releasing finger pressure maintained for 10 seconds. Among 1,467 patients analysed, normalization occurred in 85.9% with personalized resuscitation versus 61.7% with usual care. The hierarchical 28-day outcome favoured personalized care (win ratio 1.16; 95% CI 1.02–1.33; P=.04), principally through shorter organ support; 28-day mortality was 26.5% versus 26.6%. This was a resuscitation strategy, not a test of an immune-targeted drug.
milestones.set_by: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 investigators, published trial protocol and intervention algorithm.
milestones.threshold_quote: a refill time longer than 3 seconds was defined as abnormal.

milestones.title: A host-response treatment reduces 90-day mortality in a multicentre randomized septic-shock trial.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate superiority on the APROCCHSS primary endpoint, all-cause mortality at 90 days, using its two-sided significance level of 0.05. Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone met this endpoint in the 2018 report: relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.78–0.99; P=.03. Vasopressor withdrawal and recovery to SOFA <6 also occurred earlier. Hyperglycaemia was more frequent. The trial did not establish the combined 6-hour perfusion and infection-safety test specified for completion.
milestones.set_by: APROCCHSS investigators, NCT00625209, published protocol and statistical analysis plan.
milestones.threshold_quote: Ninety-day mortality was the primary endpoint.

milestones.title: One multicentre trial establishes the combined circulatory, organ-recovery, survival and infection effect.
milestones.criterion: One randomized multicentre trial of the same host-directed strategy shows increased attainment of capillary refill time ≤3 seconds during 6 hours, earlier vasopressor withdrawal with mean arterial pressure ≥60 mm Hg sustained for ≥24 hours, more days alive with SOFA <6 through day 28, and lower 90-day mortality. For infections arising ≥48 hours after randomization, the upper 95% confidence limit for the infection risk ratio is ≤1. This is the joint demonstration before independent confirmation; no cited trial establishes all these results together.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; no published outside-body criterion for this joint demonstration was located in the searched guidance, product profiles or trial protocols.

not_found: No outside-body completion test combining rapid shock reversal, organ recovery, survival and preserved infection defenses was located.
No general numerical deadline for host-directed shock reversal or accepted secondary-infection safety margin was located.
No cited trial demonstrated the complete combination with independent confirmation.
